The target reads the file from this tab as it boots. Nothing is uploaded first or put on the card, so keep the tab open meanwhile. It is slow, about 11 minutes a gigabyte, so I suggest it for images up to 1 GB. A bigger one is faster from the card or a URL. Video runs at 2 fps while the target reads.
The device opens the link itself, so it needs internet (or your NAS), not this browser.

Boot from URL leaves the image on the server: the target reads it part by part as it boots, and nothing goes onto the card. The server has to answer HTTP Range requests, as nginx, Apache, Caddy and most NAS servers do.
Download to card copies the whole file first, so it boots at card speed and without the server.

Like REISUB but powers the machine off instead of rebooting: the last step is O rather than B. Syncs and remounts read-only first, so the disks are safe.

MJPEG or H.264. The codec, quality and frame rate can be changed.
Paste text in the target's layout, one of 21, picked next to the paste box. Media keys, an on-screen keyboard, a trackpad on a phone.
[[Ctrl+K]] or [[Ctrl+Shift+P]]: type a few letters of what you want - a panel, a key combination, a macro, a setting - and press Enter.

The tab's icon shows what the device is doing, so you see it from another tab: grey when the device is unreachable, a ring during an update, a red dot while recording, a power sign when the target is off, a dash with no picture.
Pin a key like F2 or Del, a macro or a runbook to the bar under the picture.

Boot the target from an image on the microSD card, in the device's flash, on a web server or on this computer. Drop a file on the picture to put it on the card. On a device with a screen and buttons, pick the image right there.
Recordings, screenshots, a dashcam that keeps the last minutes, timelapse. On a microSD card.
Send recordings and screenshots to a WebDAV folder, such as Nextcloud or a NAS, with one button or on their own as soon as they are saved.
The target's sound, live and in recordings: from HDMI, or through a USB speaker the device offers the target.
Macros, runbooks and a scheduler. Screen areas react when a part of the screen changes.
Read a text screen, like a BIOS or a console, as characters and copy it.
Power and reset buttons over ATX wiring, the power and disk lights, Wake-on-LAN, power on over USB.
Several machines behind one device: pick one by name in the Power menu. One wire to the switch's button, or a TESmart switch over the network.
Server tools such as redfishtool and OpenStack Ironic can power the target on and off and boot it from an image at a URL. It has a password of its own.
HDMI-CEC: turn a TV or a media box on and off, use its remote.
The device can be a controller for a Nintendo Switch.
The target sends its screen over USB instead of HDMI, from OS Services running on it.
Settings for each target. The device picks one from what is attached.
The target's serial console, its log over the network, and ESP-KVM Tools for the clipboard and a clean shutdown.
Tailscale or WireGuard, to reach the device from outside without opening ports. Tailscale needs only a sign-in.
Up to three networks to join, the strongest one in sight first. Find networks lists what the device can see.
A network change that cuts the device off goes back by itself in 10 minutes. With no network for long, the device restarts.
The picture, keyboard and mouse in TigerVNC or Remmina, encrypted with VeNCrypt. Written by Jan Heil.
The device and the target's state over MQTT, found by Home Assistant by itself.
A message to Telegram, ntfy, a webhook or this browser when a phrase shows up on the screen, the screen goes blank or a new release is out.
A password, two-factor sign-in, a view-only sign-in for others, your own HTTPS certificate.
The name the target sees for the USB devices and the monitor: ESP-KVM, a plain one, or your own.
A small screen on the device that shows its state. You pick its pages, and it can go dark after a while.
The console in another language, for this browser. Downloaded when chosen, or loaded from a file on a device with no internet.
Updates over the network. A trial update goes back by itself unless you keep it.
this browser has no WebCodecs; download the file and open it in VLC

H.264 costs a fraction of the bandwidth of MJPEG on a screen that barely changes, and about a third of the frame rate. Browsers decode it through WebCodecs, which they offer on HTTPS pages only, so it is unusable over plain HTTP until TLS is in place.
Higher is sharper and larger. Only affects the MJPEG codec.
Target bitrate for the hardware encoder.

Let the console take H.264 over WebRTC: UDP, so a lost packet costs one frame instead of holding up the ones behind it. Only a signed-in console can start it, and the video is encrypted (DTLS-SRTP). Off sends all video over the WebSocket.
Upper bound on encoded frames per second. Lower it to save bandwidth on a slow link.
Stop sending while the target's screen is static. Drops the bitrate to nearly zero on an idle desktop. MJPEG only: H.264 already codes an unchanged screen as a frame of a few hundred bytes.

For VNC clients such as TigerVNC and Remmina. Set a password first. With VeNCrypt the link is encrypted (TigerVNC uses it by itself). Plain VNC is not, so use that on your own network or over Tailscale. One client at a time: a new one that signs in takes over.
5900 is what VNC clients try when no port is given.
Up to 8 characters, a limit of VNC itself, so use all 8. Latin letters, digits and symbols only. It is never shown again. Changing it disconnects the client.
Take VNC clients that connect through the device's own Wi-Fi hotspot.

The encoder's rate controller can settle at its coarsest setting and stay there: the picture goes to visible blocks on a screen that is not moving, and nothing short of building a new encoder brings it back. With this on, keyframes that collapse to a fraction of their usual size are taken as that fault and the encoder is rebuilt - a lost frame, once every two minutes at most. Turn it off if a screen of yours is being rebuilt for no reason; the log says when it happens.

What this device claims to be, as a monitor - the target picks its output mode from what is offered here. "Full" advertises the common modes from 640x480 up to 1920x1080@30. "720p" and "1024x768" stop lower, which is often what you want: a smaller picture encodes faster and costs less bandwidth. "1080p30" offers that one mode alone, for a source that refuses a list. "480p" offers 720x480 and nothing bigger, for old consoles and TV boxes. "1080p50", the default, is "Full" with 1920x1080@50 first: the target sends a frame every 20 ms instead of 33, so the pointer shows up sooner, for a frame or two a second less. It also offers 1280x1024 and 1600x900 at 60 Hz. Only boards with a rev 3.x chip and a TC358743 take 50 Hz; others get "Full". Text modes stay on offer either way, so a BIOS still comes through as text.

A long recording is written as several files, each playable on its own, so one is quick to download and a damaged card loses one piece rather than the whole. 0 starts a new file only at 3.9 GB, the largest file the device writes.
So a recording left running does not fill the card. 0 records until it is stopped or the card is full. A runbook's "record <seconds>" and the API's ?seconds= set their own length instead.
Keep the last minutes in memory

Keeps the screen's recent past in memory, and saves it to the microSD card as a clip when something happens - the screen stays one colour, a watched phrase appears, the power goes off - or when you press Save clip. How far back depends on the picture: minutes of a still screen, seconds of a playing video. Needs H.264, and keeps the encoder running while it is on. On boards with an older (pre-3.0) chip there is less memory left, so it reaches back seconds, not minutes; keep the past on the microSD card there instead.

"Memory" holds what PSRAM can spare and does not touch the card until something happens. "microSD" writes the screen to the card all the time, in 15-second pieces in VIDEO/.dashcam, and deletes the old ones: it reaches back as far as the setting below on any board, but the card cannot be handed to the target meanwhile.
At most this much of the past goes into a clip - if memory holds that much, or all of it when the past is kept on the card.
How long a clip goes on after what set it off. Another event meanwhile makes it longer, up to ten minutes in all.
Save when the screen stays one colour
Half a minute of one flat colour, such as a stop screen. A black screen does not count: that is usually the display going to sleep.
Save when a watched phrase appears
The phrases are the ones set for screen alerts.
Save when the target's power goes off
Needs the ATX power LED wired, so the device can see it.
Save the screen's text with a recording

Reads the screen as characters every few seconds while recording and writes what it says into a .txt beside the video, so the recordings panel can search it and jump to the moment. Only screens drawn as text can be read - a BIOS, an installer, a console - and reading one costs about a tenth of a second.
What a timelapse started from Home Assistant, or offered first in the recordings panel, keeps: one frame this often, played back at 25 fps.

Where the Upload button sends a recording or a screenshot: a folder on a WebDAV server, such as https://cloud.example.com/remote.php/dav/files/me/espkvm/ on Nextcloud, or a share on a NAS. Files go into a folder named after this device, with VIDEO and SCREENSHOTS in it. HTTPS needs a certificate the device trusts; plain http sends the password unencrypted, so keep it to your own network.
For the WebDAV server. Empty if it needs none.
On Nextcloud, an app password made under Settings, Security.
What goes to the WebDAV folder on its own, as soon as it is saved on the card. Files wait on the card while the server cannot be reached, also over a restart.

Writes what was pressed as subtitles next to each recording (a .srt file of the same name; VLC and mpv show it). "Keys": shortcuts, named keys and clicks, with typed characters shown as dots. "Everything": the typed text too - which includes any password typed on the target, stored on the card in plain text.
With keystrokes in recordings on, also write each mouse click and where it landed.

Read a text screen even when nobody is looking, and raise an alert when it says one of the phrases below. This is the case a KVM is bought for - a machine that fell over at three in the morning - so it keeps working with the console closed. Costs one pass over the frame a second, and only while the target is showing text.

Comma-separated, matched without regard to case, anywhere on a line - for example: no boot device, kernel panic, press F1 to continue. An alert is raised the moment one appears and cleared when it goes, and every phrase on screen is named, not only the first; the log records both, and Home Assistant gets a sensor if MQTT is on.

Which machine's conventions the console follows - the label on the Meta key, and which OS-specific key combinations it offers. "Detect" trusts the guess made from how the target enumerates USB, shown next to the USB status; set it by hand if that guess is wrong or unknown.

Absolute puts the target's cursor exactly where you click and is the right choice almost always. Relative is for software that captures the pointer, such as games and 3D viewers, and for SteamOS in game mode, where the absolute one does not move. In relative mode the console hides your own cursor while in control, so the target's is the only one; Esc gives it back.

"Click" waits for a click on the button over the picture before input reaches the target. "Click anywhere" takes any click on the picture. Either way the first click only moves the pointer there, and Esc or a click outside the picture stops. "Hover" follows the pointer as soon as it is over the picture, the way a remote desktop does, and the keyboard still needs one click.

Your own cursor over the picture, while you have control in absolute mode. "arrow" is the usual one. "dot" is a small dot, so the target's own cursor is easy to see and you still know where you point. "hidden" leaves only the target's cursor, which trails yours a little.

For a target with more than one screen, or one that puts black borders round its picture. The absolute pointer covers the whole desktop, so with two screens the cursor runs off onto the other one, and with borders it lands short of where you click. "Find this screen" fills in these four. By hand, in the picture's pixels: for two 1920x1080 screens side by side with this one on the right, 3840, 1080, 1920, 0. For a 1440x1080 desktop in the middle of a 1920x1080 picture, 1440, 1080, -240, 0. 0 here turns it off.
The height of the whole desktop. 0 means the same as this screen.
Where this screen starts, from the left of the whole desktop. Below 0 when the desktop starts to the right of the picture's left edge (black borders).
Where this screen starts, from the top of the whole desktop. Below 0 when the desktop starts below the picture's top edge (black borders).
Scales pointer movement in relative mode only.

0 turns it off. Otherwise the pointer is nudged one pixel and put straight back this often, so the target does not lock or fall asleep while you are watching it. It stands aside whenever you are using the mouse yourself, and does nothing when no target is attached.

For an old BIOS that does not see the keyboard. The target then gets one plain keyboard at USB 1.1 speed, the way a real keyboard looks. The mouse, media keys and virtual media are off while this is on. Takes effect after a restart.

A game controller for the target, and a gamepad panel in the console; a controller plugged into your own computer works through it too. "Nintendo Switch": a HORI Pokken pad. "Xbox 360 (XInput)": a wired Xbox 360 pad, for Windows, a Steam Deck and Linux. "Original Xbox": the original Xbox pad, always alone; the console's controller port needs an adapter to a USB socket. The pad joins the keyboard and mouse; the "pad only" choices show the pad and nothing else, the way the real one looks - Windows needs that for the Xbox pad, and a console may ignore a pad with company. Takes effect after a restart.
How far the target scrolls for a turn of the wheel or a swipe on a touchpad. 100 sends one wheel click per notch, 50 one per two notches.

Used when pasting text and in macros, so the characters sent match what the target types. A KVM sends key positions, not characters. Where Windows and Linux place a character differently, the target OS setting decides.
Raise it if the target drops characters while text is being pasted.
Saved macros, edited from the Input panel.
Buttons pinned to the console's bar, edited from the Input panel.
Saved runbooks, edited from the Runbooks panel.
Let the device fire scheduled actions. It needs the clock set over the network.
Set the clock over the network
Recordings and screenshots are named by the clock, and schedules run by it. Without this, the console sets the clock when you sign in. Schedules set it over the network anyway.
Where the clock is set from. A name on the local network works with no internet.
Pick your city; the browser's own zone is at the top of the list. File names and schedules use it. Stored as a POSIX TZ string, e.g. MSK-3 or CET-1CEST,M3.5.0,M10.5.0/3.

A battery-backed clock module keeps the time through a restart with no network. Auto finds a DS3231 (or DS3231M, DS3232) and a PCF8563 or BM8563. A PCF85063 or PCF8523 shares an address with something else and must be named here. Off leaves the bus alone. Only the DS3231 has been tried on hardware.

Where the module is wired. The capture board's I2C is pins 3 (SDA) and 5 (SCL) of the 40-pin header on most boards, and a DS3231 for Raspberry Pi plugs straight on there. Own pins puts it on a second I2C bus.
The data line of the clock module's own bus.
The clock line of the clock module's own bus.
Saved schedules, edited from the Automation panel.
Send a message when something happens on the target: a watched phrase, a blank screen, a dashcam clip. The table below picks what goes where.
Send the screen with the message, where the channel can carry a picture.
Include the tail of the device log with the message - the context around an alert.
From @BotFather, like 123456:AA... . Message the bot once so it may write to you.
The chat to message. Find chats lists the ones that wrote to the bot lately; a group or channel id typed in works too.

A URL to POST a small JSON message to. The body is {"title":"...","message":"...","device":"<hostname>"}, with a "log" field added when the log tail is switched on above, sent as application/json; anything answering 2xx counts as delivered. Optional.

The topic to post to, such as https://ntfy.sh/a-long-name-nobody-guesses, or a topic on your own ntfy server. Subscribe to the same topic in the ntfy app. Anyone who knows a topic on ntfy.sh can read it, so pick a long name. Optional.
For a topic that needs a login: an access token (tk_...), or user:password. Empty if it needs none.
A dashcam clip under 50 MB plays in the chat. A bigger one is named.
A dashcam clip is named, with its file on the card.
Text only: a push message has no room for a picture.
The screenshot goes as an attachment where the server takes them, else the text alone. A dashcam clip is named, with its file on the card.

Present a USB drive to the target that it can boot from. Off keeps the device a plain keyboard and mouse, which also frees the USB endpoints the drive would use. Adding or removing the drive re-enumerates the device to the target, so it takes effect after a restart; swapping the image once the drive exists does not.

How an image is presented to the target. "Auto" serves a .iso as a CD-ROM (so it boots and mounts as an optical drive) and any other file as a removable disk - the right choice almost always. Force "CD-ROM" or "Disk" only if a file is misnamed. Handing over the whole card is picked in the Media panel, not here. Switching the type re-attaches the USB drive.

The fastest clock the card is tried at. "Auto" starts at what the board supports and steps down by itself when the card fails to mount, fails a test read, or fails a transfer later. Pick a lower one for a card that keeps stepping down. Takes effect after a restart.
File on the microSD card currently offered to the target.

An image on a web server that the target boots without it being copied to the card, used while the mounted image is "@url". The server must answer HTTP Range requests. Secret: a link may carry a password or a signed token.
The target's Ethernet MAC, e.g. AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF. The Wake button sends it a magic packet. The target must have Wake-on-LAN enabled in its BIOS and keep standby power.

Talk to the target over the HDMI cable's CEC line: see what is connected, put it to sleep, wake it and send remote-control keys. Works with TV boxes, consoles, a Raspberry Pi; most PCs do not speak CEC.
Requires optocouplers wired to the target's front-panel header.
Drives the optocoupler across the target's power button. -1 to disable.
Drives the optocoupler across the target's reset button. -1 to disable.
Reads the target's power LED through an optocoupler. Wire it to the power LED, not the HDD LED, which only blinks on disk activity. -1 if you are not sensing the LED.
Reads the target's HDD LED the same way as the power LED, and with the same active-high setting. The power button in the console then blinks while the disk works. -1 if you are not sensing it.
How long a normal power or reset press is held.
How long the power button is held for a hard power off.
On to press the button when the GPIO drives high (high-level-trigger optocoupler modules). Turn off if your module presses on a low.
On if the LED sense reads high when the target is powered. Flip it if the reported power state is inverted.

A KVM switch between this device and several machines, so the console's Power menu lists them. "button": a GPIO wired to the switch's select button, each press moves it to the next machine. "tesmart": a TESmart switch told the machine over the network, no wires.
Wired to the switch's select button. -1 to leave it unwired.
The TESmart switch's address on the network, with :port if it is not 5000. A new switch is at 192.168.1.10. It has no password, so keep it on a network you trust.

On when the GPIO goes straight to the side of the switch's button that is not ground, with the grounds joined: a press pulls it low, and between presses the pin lets go. Only if that side is at 3.3 V or less. Off for an optocoupler module that presses on a high.
How many machines the switch has.
Names for the console, in the switch's order, split by commas. For example: NAS, Desktop. Empty gives Machine 1, Machine 2.
How long each press of the switch's button is held.

Optional. Reads the switch's light for the first machine, so the device knows where the switch is after someone presses its button by hand. Without it the device counts its own presses from the first machine. -1 if not wired.
On if the LED input reads high while the first machine is selected.

The target's serial port, for a machine with no screen at all - a NAS, a router, a server - or one that shows its BIOS over serial. Wire the target's TX to the RX pin below and its RX to the TX pin, plus ground. 3.3 V logic (a Raspberry Pi, a router's header) goes straight in; a real RS-232 port (9-pin, +-12 V) needs a MAX3232 module in between, or it damages the pin.

A serial port on the USB cable the target already has, so no wires. Linux sees it as /dev/ttyACM0, Windows as a COM port, macOS as /dev/cu.usbmodem*. "Serial console": the serial console uses it instead of the pins below; on Linux run a login on it with "systemctl enable --now serial-getty@ttyACM0". "ESP-KVM Tools": for the small program of that name on the target, which shows what the machine is and shares its clipboard. Not together with a gamepad. Takes effect after a restart.
The GPIO this device sends on. -1 until you pick one.
The GPIO this device listens on. -1 until you pick one.
What the target's console runs at; 115200 for Linux and most boards, 9600 or 115200 for a PC BIOS. Always 8 data bits, no parity, one stop bit.

The capture board sends the HDMI sound as I2S on three wires: bit clock (BCLK or SCK), word clock (WS, LRCK or WFS) and data (SD or DATA). Wire them to three free pins, plus ground, and pick those pins below. On the Geekworm C790 they are on the J4 header.

For a board that cannot take the sound from HDMI. The target gets a USB speaker, "ESP-KVM Speaker"; pick it as the sound output there, and what it plays comes to the console and the recordings. The target's own speakers go quiet while it is picked, and a BIOS plays nothing to it. When on, it is used instead of HDMI audio. Takes effect after a restart.
A quiet knock-knock on the board's own speaker when a console is opened, at most once in 30 s. Needs a speaker on the board's speaker connector.
Say on the network that this is an ESP-KVM

Adds the product and the board to the mDNS announcement, and an _espkvm._tcp service, so a discovery tool or a script can find every ESP-KVM on the network. Off, only the hostname is announced. The firmware version is never announced.
Also answer on an IPv6 address, alongside IPv4. There is nothing to configure: the address comes from the router's advertisements. Turn it off to keep the device off IPv6 entirely.

"Ethernet": the wired port. "WiFi": join the network below (Ethernet is left down). "Own hotspot": the device makes its own WiFi hotspot for setup where there is no network to join. "Ethernet, WiFi as backup": the wired port, with the WiFi network below joined and waiting - when the cable is pulled the device moves to WiFi, and back when the cable returns. It answers on both addresses. If WiFi is unreachable: reset the board, then hold the button for two seconds - that returns it to Ethernet, and clears the password too. Hold it AFTER the reset, not through it.
The name of the network to join in WiFi mode.
Left blank for an open network. Stored write-only.
Another network the device knows, such as at a second site. With more than one, it joins the strongest one in range, and moves on when that one goes. Optional.

Run the device's hotspot with no password at all. Off, and with no password set, the device makes one up on first use and prints it in the log and on the display - an open network anybody in the building can join is a poor way to reach a server. Turn this on only where that is what you want.

Password for the device's own hotspot ("Own hotspot" mode, or the rescue hotspot below). At least 8 characters. Left blank, the device makes one up the first time the hotspot comes up and prints it in the log and on the display; for a hotspot with no password at all, use the setting above. The network name is ESP-KVM-xxxx (the device's MAC). Stored write-only.

"Keep trying": keep retrying the network - it reconnects on its own when the network comes back (best for a device you cannot reach physically). "Also start a hotspot": ALSO run a rescue hotspot (ESP-KVM-xxxx) the whole time WiFi is trying, so you can always reach the device on-site to fix its settings - set a Hotspot password first. Only applies in WiFi (station) mode.
Setup hotspot on an unclaimed device

While no password has been set and no network cable is plugged in, put out an open hotspot (ESP-KVM-xxxx) so the device can be reached and given one. It stops happening the moment a password exists. Until then a visitor can only set that password - video, keyboard and every other endpoint stay shut.
Undo a network change that cuts the device off

After a change to Wi-Fi, the address, Tailscale or WireGuard, the device checks for 10 minutes that it is still on the network (and on the VPN, if the change came over it). If not, it puts the old settings back and restarts. Opening the console in that time also keeps the change.
Restart when the network is gone for long

With no working network for 30 minutes, the device restarts, then waits longer each time: 1, 2 and 4 hours, then every 6 hours. It does not restart while a recording runs or while the Ethernet cable is simply unplugged. If the Wi-Fi chip does not start at all, the first restarts come after 2 and 5 minutes.

Listen for the target's kernel messages over the network: Linux netconsole, or anything that sends plain syslog over UDP. It keeps working when the target's disk is gone, which is when you want it. On the target, for example: modprobe netconsole netconsole=@/,6666@<this device's IP>/. What arrives is unauthenticated UDP - anyone on the network can read it or send lines - so it is kept as text and can only raise a notification, never run anything.
6666 is netconsole's usual port; 514 is syslog's.
The target's IP address; several separated by commas. Empty accepts lines from anyone on the network.
Comma-separated phrases, matched without regard to case. A line holding one sends a notification, at most one every 30 seconds. Empty for none.

Bring up a classic WireGuard tunnel to a hub so the device is reachable over the VPN. Off by default. Split-tunnel: only the tunnel subnet goes through WireGuard, so the console stays reachable on the LAN too. An alternative to Tailscale below, not a companion - enable one.
The device's own IP on the WireGuard network, e.g. 10.9.0.2.
Base64 WireGuard private key. Leave empty and the device generates one on first connect; its public key is shown below.
Base64 public key of the WireGuard peer (the hub/server).
host:port of the peer, e.g. vpn.example.com:51820.
Keeps a NAT/firewall mapping open. 25 is typical; 0 disables it.
WireGuard handshakes carry a timestamp; without a real clock a reboot can make the peer reject them. Turn this on if the device can reach an NTP server. Off by default (isolated networks).
Used only when SNTP is on.

Join a Tailscale network natively - the device gets a 100.x address reachable from anywhere on your tailnet, with NAT traversal handled for you and no separate gateway. Off by default. An alternative to WireGuard above, not a companion; enabling both is unusual.

Optional. A Tailscale auth key (tskey-auth-...) or a Headscale one (hskey-auth-...) that authorises this device to join. Empty, the device shows a link to sign in with your Tailscale account instead. Generate a key in the Tailscale admin console. A reusable key survives re-registration across reboots.
The name this device takes on the tailnet. Empty uses the mDNS hostname from the Network section.

While the device is on the tailnet, the console answers only to tailnet addresses (100.64.0.0/10). The setup hotspot still works, and while Tailscale is down the console answers everywhere again, so a broken tailnet cannot lock you out.

Tailscale logins, separated by commas (alice@example.com). A browser on a device of one of these users is signed in as the owner without a password or a code. Works once a password of your own is set. Signing out there signs straight back in.
Tailscale logins, separated by commas. These are signed in as the viewer: they see the screen and cannot type, click or change anything.

Coordination server for a self-hosted control plane (Headscale, Ionscale). Empty uses Tailscale's own (controlplane.tailscale.com). A host (headscale.example.com) or a URL (https://headscale.example.com:8443), which then sets TLS and the port too.
Port for the control server. 0 = default (443 with TLS, else 80). Set only if your Headscale listens on a non-standard port.
Reach the coordination server over HTTPS. Required for the hosted Tailscale service (the default). Turn off only for a self-hosted Headscale served over plain HTTP.
Warn before the key runs out

Send a notification this many days before the tailnet key expires. Tailscale gives a node six months at most, and when that runs out the device drops off the tailnet until someone authorises it again. 0 turns the warning off. Needs notifications set up and the clock in sync.

Get a Let's Encrypt certificate for the device's tailnet name (host.tailnet.ts.net) and renew it on its own, so a browser trusts the console with nothing imported. Needs MagicDNS and HTTPS certificates turned on in the Tailscale admin console (DNS page). The name is published in Certificate Transparency logs. The local name and the IP addresses keep the device's own certificate.
Report status to an MQTT broker and appear in Home Assistant (auto-discovered). Off by default; costs nothing when off.
Hostname or IP of the MQTT broker, e.g. the Home Assistant host.
1883 for plain MQTT, 8883 for MQTT over TLS.
Connect with mqtts. Set the port to 8883 as well.
With TLS on, check the broker's certificate against the built-in CA bundle (public CAs, e.g. Let's Encrypt). Turn off for a broker with a self-signed certificate.
Leave empty for an anonymous broker.
Stored on the device; never sent back to the console.
Topic prefix; the device id is appended, e.g. espkvm/a1b2c3.
Home Assistant MQTT discovery prefix. Default suits a stock HA.
Send a picture with a screen alert

When the screen watch fires, publish a still of the screen as a camera in Home Assistant, so the notification carries what the machine actually shows. The button is always there; this only decides whether an alert takes a picture by itself. Works on either codec, and a 1080p frame is a few hundred kilobytes over the broker.
Uses a self-signed certificate generated on first boot. Disable only on a trusted network or behind a VPN.

Enables the plain-REST snapshot and keyboard/mouse endpoints (/api/v1/video/frame.jpg, /api/v1/hid/*) used to drive the target from an AI agent or a script. Off by default: it grants the same control the console already has, over a simpler interface, so turn it on only when you mean to hand that control to a program.

The server-management API of iDRAC and iLO, at /redfish/v1, for tools such as redfishtool and OpenStack Ironic. It can power the target on and off through the ATX wiring (without it, only wake it) and boot it from an image at a URL. Tools sign in with any user name and the Redfish password below.
Its own password, not the console's: it opens power and virtual media only. Use a long random one. It is never shown again.
What the target's device list calls this device. "Plain": Generic USB Device, USB Disk, USB Speaker. "Custom": names and USB IDs of your own. Takes effect after a restart.
Up to 32 plain Latin characters. The virtual drive shows the first 8. Empty: ESP-KVM.
Up to 32 plain Latin characters. The virtual drive shows the first 16. Empty: ESP-KVM.
Empty: made from the device's MAC address, so it differs between devices.
4 hex digits. 303A is Espressif's. ESP-KVM Tools on the target finds the device by these IDs, so with other IDs it does not see it. Use only an ID that is yours to use.

4 hex digits. Empty: one of 4012, 4013, 4032 or 4033, by the serial port and speaker settings. A set ID stays the same when those change, and Windows may then need the device removed in Device Manager once.

What the target's display settings call this device. "Plain": a monitor named HDMI, with no product code or serial number. "Custom": a name and codes of your own. A change makes it a new monitor to the target, which may then pick another resolution. Takes effect after a restart.
Up to 13 plain Latin characters. Empty: ESP-KVM.
3 letters, the maker's PnP ID, such as ESP. Empty: ESP.

The browser asks the address below whether a newer build exists and offers to install it. With the project's own address it also tells check.espkvm.io, once a day and again after an update, this device's random id, its board, its version and the chip revision, so the author can count the devices in use. The counts also go on to Google Analytics, under a hash of the id, never the id or your address. The id is not taken from the hardware; erasing the flash makes a new one. The device itself asks only when New firmware is ticked for a channel under Notifications: once a day, and it sends nothing about itself when it does.

URL of a manifest.json describing the newest build. The project's own builds are published at the default address; point it at your fork, or at a file server inside your network, and it will use that instead. Whatever it points at is what gets written to the device, so point it somewhere you trust.
Let the device fetch releases itself

Off by default, and deliberately so: a KVM often sits where nothing is supposed to reach the internet, and it does not talk to GitHub unless it is told to. Turn it on and the console can offer any published release - which is how you go back to an earlier one, since the browser is not allowed to download the image itself. Ordinary updates do not need this; the browser fetches those and hands them over.

Cap the frame rate when the chip gets warm and stop encoding if it gets hot. Keyboard, mouse and the web interface keep running either way - a KVM that stops accepting keystrokes because it is warm has failed at its job.
Above this the frame rate is halved. Measured on this board: 1080p MJPEG at full rate settles around 46 C in open air, so the default leaves plenty of room before anything is given up.
Above this encoding stops until the chip cools. The ESP32 family is rated to 85 C ambient and the die runs hotter than the air around it.
Which side of the screen the button rail and its panels sit on.
The last few keys and key combinations that went to the target, in the bottom bar. Handy when the target seems to ignore a key, or to show someone what you press.
Hide the bars in full screen

In full screen the status strip, the rail and the bottom bar slide away and the picture takes the whole screen. They come back over it with the mouse at an edge (after a moment while you have control), the small tab at the top, or a tap of the right Ctrl key on its own, and go again a few seconds after you leave them.

What the keyboard button under the picture opens in touch mode. "Console" is the console's own keyboard, with Ctrl, Alt, the F keys and the arrows a phone's keyboard does not have. "Phone" is the phone's own keyboard, for typing text with its layouts and suggestions.

Untick a control to take its button out of the console, for everyone who signs in. It only hides the button: the feature itself stays as its own settings have it. Stored as the ids of the hidden controls; the console keeps the list of what can be hidden.
A short tick under the finger on each press of the on-screen keyboard, the arrow keys and the gamepad buttons, like a phone's own keyboard. Android only: Safari on an iPhone cannot vibrate.
In touch mode, a faint tick every few millimetres the finger travels, the way the touchpads of the Steam Controller feel. Half the strength of a key press.
A browser cannot set how strong a vibration is, only how long, so stronger means a longer tick: about 12, 25 or 45 ms.

Drive a small display that shows the IP, link, capture status and health. An I2C OLED (SSD1306/SH1106) shares the capture chip's I2C and is auto-detected with no extra pins; an SPI LCD (GC9A01, ST7789) uses the GPIOs set below, after you pick it as the display type. Off by default; does nothing when no panel is connected.

Which panel is wired, controller and size together. SSD1306 and SH1106 are I2C OLEDs - pick SH1106 if the image is shifted by two pixels or wraps. GC9A01 is a round colour SPI LCD, e.g. the Waveshare 1.28" module. ST7789 is the square colour LCD built into the JetKVM Mini. None of this can be detected: one chip drives every size and reports none of it. A wrong size shows the picture squeezed into part of the glass, or every other row missing. Shorter panels show fewer status lines.
How bright the backlight of a colour SPI LCD is. Takes effect at once. Needs the backlight pin set, and does nothing on the OLEDs.
How long each status page stays up before the next one. 0 keeps the page until you press the display button.
The screen goes dark after this long, and the display button wakes it on the page it had. An update or a notice lights it too. 0 keeps it on.
A sleeping screen lights up when a console is opened, so whoever stands at the device sees that someone connected.

Turn the picture on the OLED through 180 degrees, for a panel mounted the other way up because of where its connector or its enclosure put it. Takes effect at once: the panel is re-initialised where it stands, with no restart.
Turn the picture on the square colour panel by a quarter, a half or three quarters, for a panel mounted on its side or the other way up. Takes effect at once, with no restart.

Which status pages the display shows. The picture page is a small copy of the target's screen on a colour panel; it redraws ten times a second, or twice while a browser is watching. With none ticked the network page stays. The Wi-Fi join code still comes up in hotspot mode.
SPI clock GPIO for the SPI LCD. Ignored by the I2C OLEDs.
SPI data GPIO for the SPI LCD.
Chip-select GPIO for the SPI LCD.
Data/command GPIO for the SPI LCD.
Reset GPIO for the SPI LCD. -1 (None) if RST is tied to 3V3.

I2C data GPIO for an OLED on a bus of its own, such as the Grove port of the M5Stack Unit PoE-P4. -1 (None) puts the OLED on the capture chip's bus, where most boards have it. Set both SDA and SCL, or neither.
I2C clock GPIO for an OLED on a bus of its own. -1 (None) puts it on the capture chip's bus.
Backlight GPIO for the SPI LCD. -1 (None) if BL is tied to 3V3 (always on).

The picture, and what is recorded from it.
The target's sound, on three wires from the capture board.
Keyboard and pointer, as the target sees them.
The microSD card and what is offered to the target.
ATX wiring, Wake-on-LAN, HDMI-CEC and the serial console.
Push buttons wired to the device, and what a press or a hold of each does.
One tunnel at a time: WireGuard or Tailscale.
Reporting to a home automation system.
Where the device sends news of its own accord.
